Think of your graphics card’s memory as a massive, high-speed highway where data travels. When you run a standard AI model, that data is usually stored in a format called FP32, which is like a high-precision GPS system. It gives you incredibly detailed coordinates, but it’s heavy. Every single number takes up four bytes of space, meaning your GPU’s memory gets clogged up fast, and the data bus has to shuttle around a lot of bulky information. This is where quantization comes in, and it’s essentially the process of compressing that data without losing the core meaning. Imagine you’re trying to describe a location to a friend. Instead of giving them the exact latitude and longitude down to the nanometer, you just say, "It’s in the middle of the park, near the fountain." You’ve lost some precision, but you’ve conveyed the essential point using far fewer words. In the world of AI, we do something similar by converting those heavy FP32 numbers into lighter formats, like FP16 or even INT8.
